# Leveraged ETF Risk Analytics

How does a fund that resets to twice its underlying every trading day behave
over a one-year holding period, compared with the underlying and with twice its
return? This CS544 independent project replays a daily-reset 1x/2x model on the
daily return history of NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, TSLA and QQQ over 252-trading-day
windows, runs it in PySpark with full-scale checks, and analyzes the results
with Spark SQL. The results describe historical windows of a few tickers; they
are not forecasts, and the model ignores fees, financing and execution.

## Status

| Part | Status |
|---|---|
| Data: download with manifest, checksum-enforced ingest, validation, daily returns in Parquet | Implemented |
| Model and Spark pipeline: 252-day windows on a shared trading-day grid, 1x and 2x for each window, full-scale checks, an independent sample check, measurement tooling | Implemented |
| Three Spark SQL analyses of the results ([`analysis/`](analysis/)) | Implemented |
| Docker image for the pipeline | Implemented |
| Stride experiment: runtime and memory at strides 21, 14 and 7 ([docs/experiments.md](docs/experiments.md)) | Complete; drift detected, stride 3 exploratory only |
| Shuffle-partition experiment: three Spark partition settings at stride 7 ([docs/partition-experiment.md](docs/partition-experiment.md)) | Complete; B (200 partitions, coalescing off) slower than A and C; no clear memory difference; outputs within tolerance |
| Pandas baseline: the Spark pipeline against a single-process pandas implementation, end to end, at stride 7 ([docs/pandas-baseline.md](docs/pandas-baseline.md)) | Complete; pandas had a 41.8% shorter median wall time and a 26.6% lower median peak total RSS; outputs within tolerance |
| Caching experiment: no cache, the window-member rows, and those plus the four read-back tables, at stride 7 ([docs/caching-experiment.md](docs/caching-experiment.md)) | Complete; no clear difference in runtime or peak memory; outputs within tolerance |
| Figures and final write-up | Planned |
| Optional systems extension: MySQL job table, Kafka job queue, Redis result cache | Planned ([spec](docs/spec.md), §11) |

## Reading guide

1. **This README**: status, key results and how to run everything.
2. **[docs/spec.md](docs/spec.md)**: the research questions (§2), the model and
   its assumptions (§3), how results are checked (§6), the window design (§7),
   the full results of the stride-21 run and summaries of the stride,
   shuffle-partition and caching experiments and the pandas baseline (§8).
3. **[docs/data-sources.md](docs/data-sources.md)**: where the data comes from,
   the checks run on it, and what is not verified.
4. **[docs/experiments.md](docs/experiments.md)**: the stride experiment, with
   its design and predictions (committed before any measured run), run log,
   deviations, measurements and answers;
   [`collect_measurements.py`](analysis/collect_measurements.py) builds its
   measurements CSV from the run records.
5. **[docs/partition-experiment.md](docs/partition-experiment.md)**: the
   shuffle-partition experiment, with its design, rules and predictions
   (committed before any measured run), run log, deviations, measurements,
   plans and answers; the [session helpers](docs/partition-session.zsh) ran
   its session, and the [collector](analysis/collect_partition_measurements.py)
   builds its measurements CSV and checks its acceptance criteria.
6. **[docs/pandas-baseline.md](docs/pandas-baseline.md)**: the pandas
   baseline, an end-to-end comparison of the Spark pipeline with a
   single-process pandas implementation of the same computation, with its
   design, rules and predictions (committed before any measured run), run log,
   measurements and answers; the [session helpers](docs/baseline-session.zsh)
   ran its session, and the
   [collector](analysis/collect_baseline_measurements.py) builds its
   measurements CSV and checks its acceptance criteria.
7. **[docs/caching-experiment.md](docs/caching-experiment.md)**: the caching
   experiment, which compared no cache, a cache of the window-member rows, and
   one of those rows plus the four read-back tables, with its design, rules and
   predictions (committed before any measured run), run log, measurements,
   cache checks and answers; the [session helpers](docs/caching-session.zsh)
   ran its session, and the
   [collector](analysis/collect_caching_measurements.py) builds its
   measurements CSV and checks its acceptance criteria.
8. **The analyses**: [`sql_overview.py`](analysis/sql_overview.py) (counts and
   medians per ticker), [`sql_comparison.py`](analysis/sql_comparison.py) (how
   often 2x beats twice the 1x return) and
   [`sql_sensitivity.py`](analysis/sql_sensitivity.py) (medians without the
   windows that use an unverified day).
9. **The code**, in data-flow order: in `src/etf_risk/`, `download` → `ingest`
   (with `validate`) → `windows` → `spark_pipeline` (which runs `model`) →
   `verify`; `measure` times runs, `plans` records a run's execution plans,
   and `pandas_pipeline` computes the same results in one process without
   Spark. Module overview: spec §5.
10. **How AI was used**: [AI assistance](#ai-assistance) below.

## Key results

From the run of record: snapshot `full-2026-10-12` (daily history through
2025-12-31), 252-day windows starting every 21 trading days. The windows
overlap, so these numbers describe one history, not independent samples; spec
§8 has the details.

- All 46 check tests passed with no violation on 1,790 windows, and the
  independent Python check matched all 1,074 paths it compared. Every window
  without a breach (1,778) passes the two identity checks of the 2x model (exact
  log gap, drawdown bound).
- 12 AAPL windows breach at 2x (a daily loss of 50% or more); all contain
  2000-09-29, a day not yet checked against a second source. They have no 2x
  return and are left out of the 2x statistics below.

| | AAPL | MSFT | NVDA | TSLA | QQQ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | 529 | 466 | 311 | 174 | 310 |
| Median 1x return | 24.4% | 22.8% | 39.5% | 22.5% | 16.6% |
| Median 2x return | 35.2% (517 windows) | 39.9% | 51.3% | 13.5% | 31.4% |
| 2x return above twice the 1x return | 219 of 517 (42.4%) | 164 of 466 (35.2%) | 141 of 311 (45.3%) | 43 of 174 (24.7%) | 140 of 310 (45.2%) |
| Windows using an unverified extreme day | 78 | 12 | 92 | 57 | 0 |
| Median 2x return without those windows | 48.5% (451) | 41.4% (454) | 52.2% (219) | −12.3% (117) | 31.4% (310) |

- For every ticker, the daily-reset 2x return exceeded twice the 1x return in
  fewer than half of the windows.
- The last row is a sensitivity analysis: TSLA's 2x median falls from 13.5% to
  −12.3%, while AAPL's rises from 35.2% to 48.5%. It shows how much a result
  depends on periods with extreme days, not whether those days are data errors.
- Runtime and memory were measured on one Apple Silicon laptop (8 cores, 8 GiB
  RAM), with Spark in local mode and, apart from the shuffle-partition
  experiment, default settings; the numbers describe that machine and those
  configurations, not others. For the run of record, the median wall time over
  three measured runs was 44.7 s and the median peak memory 1.27 GiB (summed
  resident memory of the run's processes, sampled every 0.25 s).
- The stride experiment ([docs/experiments.md](docs/experiments.md)) measured
  the same stride-21 workload and strides 14 and 7 (1.5 and 3 times the
  windows) on 2026-10-19: median wall times 22.2, 20.3 and 25.7 s, median
  peaks 2.62 to 2.70 GiB, and every check passed in all 20 runs. At stride 21
  that is half the run of record's time and about twice its memory, with more
  memory free before the runs; the records do not establish why. A linear fit
  over the three strides gives an intercept of 18.8 s (85% of the stride-21
  median) and 1.2 ms per window: an estimate from three points, not measured
  overhead. A repeated stride-21 protocol at the end had an 18.3% shorter
  median wall time than the first, beyond the 10% drift tolerance, so
  comparisons across strides are marked as affected. Stride 3 was run although
  the experiment's memory rule did not admit it; its results (40.2 s,
  2.73 GiB) are exploratory only.
- The shuffle-partition experiment
  ([docs/partition-experiment.md](docs/partition-experiment.md)) ran the
  stride-7 workload on 2026-10-22 (UTC) with three settings: A, Spark's
  defaults (200 shuffle partitions, AQE coalescing on); B, 200 partitions with
  coalescing off; C, 8 partitions with coalescing off. Eight runs each, in the
  order A–B–C–C–B–A, all passed every check. Median times without the plan
  recording were 26.5, 44.6 and 25.3 s: B's was 69% longer than A's and 77%
  longer than C's, in the same direction in both halves of the order, while A
  and C showed no clear difference. Median peaks were 2.69 GiB in all three,
  and `paired` and `path_summary` matched A's within the tolerance. In B, one
  join stayed a sort-merge join where AQE chose a broadcast join in A and C.
  No drift was detected; the machine checks were recorded only before the
  first protocol, and the last protocol followed a two-hour break.
- The pandas baseline
  ([docs/pandas-baseline.md](docs/pandas-baseline.md)) compared the Spark
  pipeline at Spark's defaults end to end with a single-process pandas
  implementation of the same computation, on the stride-7 workload on
  2026-10-22 (UTC): eight runs each, in the order Spark–pandas–pandas–Spark,
  all passing every check. The pandas implementation's median wall time was
  15.4 s against Spark's 26.4 s (41.8% shorter), and its median peak total RSS
  1.97 against 2.68 GiB (26.6% lower), in the same direction in both halves of
  the order; its outputs matched Spark's within the tolerance. Its model phase
  took longer than Spark's and its other phases less time. Both call the same
  model function but handle data, aggregate and write in their own ways, so
  the comparison does not isolate Spark's overhead. The prediction had put
  pandas at about 40 s, slower than Spark; no drift was detected.
- The caching experiment
  ([docs/caching-experiment.md](docs/caching-experiment.md)) ran the stride-7
  workload on 2026-10-22 (UTC) with three caching strategies: A, no cache; B,
  the window-member rows cached from the window statistics through the model
  phase; C, those rows and the four tables read back after each phase, cached
  through the checks. Eight runs each, in the order A–B–C–C–B–A, all passed
  every check, and Spark's storage information and the execution plans
  verified every cache's fill and release and the cached reads in each phase.
  Median times without the plan recording were 26.5, 27.0 and 28.7 s: B's and
  C's were 2.1% and 8.4% longer than A's, below the 10% threshold, so there was
  no clear difference. Caching the members lengthened the window statistics by
  0.9 s and shortened the model phase by 0.3 s; C's further caches lengthened
  the model phase by 1.3 s, with no observed net saving in the later phases.
  Median peaks were 2.68–2.70 GiB, with C's caches, about 0.2 GiB, held in the
  JVM heap. All outputs matched A's within the tolerance; in B and C, seven
  floating-point summary columns differed in the last bits, and a different
  order of addition is a plausible but unestablished explanation. No drift was
  detected.

## Running

Requires Python 3.12, Java 17 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/); run the
commands from the repository root. Memory use has been measured on one machine
only (see Key results): there, runs at strides 21 to 7 peaked at 1.2 to 2.8 GiB,
and the exploratory stride-3 runs at up to 2.8 GiB; other machines, and Spark
settings beyond the shuffle-partition experiment's three, have not been
measured.

```bash
uv sync                                    # .venv from uv.lock
uv run --group measure pytest              # tests, no network

# 1. Download a snapshot (network). Set SNAPSHOT once; the later steps use it.
SNAPSHOT=full-$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
uv run --group download python -m etf_risk.download \
    --tickers NVDA AAPL MSFT TSLA QQQ --out data/raw/yahoo/$SNAPSHOT
# 2. Check the prices, then write daily returns       -> data/processed/$SNAPSHOT/
uv run python -m etf_risk.ingest --raw-dir data/raw/yahoo/$SNAPSHOT
# 3. Define 252-day windows at stride 21              -> data/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21/
uv run python -m etf_risk.windows --snapshot $SNAPSHOT --kind rolling --stride 21
# 4. Run the model in Spark; every check runs at full scale -> $RUN
RUN=data/outputs/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21/first
uv run python -m etf_risk.spark_pipeline --windows data/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21 --run-id first
# 5. Compare a sample of windows with an independent Python computation
uv run python -m etf_risk.verify --run $RUN
# 6. The three SQL analyses of the run
uv run python analysis/sql_overview.py $RUN
uv run python analysis/sql_comparison.py $RUN
uv run python analysis/sql_sensitivity.py $RUN
```

Optional steps, with the same variables:

```bash
# Calendar-year windows, a labeled supplement
uv run python -m etf_risk.windows --snapshot $SNAPSHOT --kind calendar-year
uv run python -m etf_risk.spark_pipeline --windows data/windows/$SNAPSHOT/calendar-year --run-id first
# Timed runs with peak memory: a fresh process per run; no further run once 60% of RAM is crossed
uv run --group measure python -m etf_risk.measure --repeats 4 -- --windows data/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21
```

- Unless `--end` is changed, the download stops at 2025-12-31, the same range as
  the run of record. Yahoo can revise adjusted prices, so a new snapshot can
  differ slightly ([data-sources.md](docs/data-sources.md)).
- Nothing is overwritten: `windows` refuses an existing folder (unless
  `--overwrite`), and `spark_pipeline` asks for a new `--run-id`.
- `spark_pipeline` also takes `--shuffle-partitions N` and `--coalesce on|off`
  (Spark settings, refused inside an existing Spark session) and
  `--record-plans`, which writes `plans.json` with the run's final plans and
  the partition counts Spark used
  ([partition-experiment.md](docs/partition-experiment.md) 4).
- `spark_pipeline --cache none|members|members-checks` caches the
  window-member rows, or those and the four read-back tables, and records the
  fills, releases and Spark's storage information in `run.json`
  ([caching-experiment.md](docs/caching-experiment.md) 4).
- `etf_risk.pandas_pipeline` takes `--windows`, `--out-root` and `--run-id`
  and writes the Spark pipeline's outputs from one process, without Spark;
  `etf_risk.measure --pipeline pandas` times it
  ([pandas-baseline.md](docs/pandas-baseline.md) 4).
- Strides below 21 need `--allow-dense-stride`. Strides 14, 7 and 3 were
  measured in the stride experiment (stride 3 as exploratory only); stride 1
  has not been run.
- The 2020–2025 prototype regression needs the prototype CSVs, which were
  downloaded outside this repository ([data-sources.md](docs/data-sources.md)).

### Docker

The image holds the code, Python 3.12, Java 17 and the locked dependencies. Data
is never copied into it: `docker/run.sh` mounts `data/processed` and
`data/windows` read-only and writes container results to `data/outputs-docker`
and `data/windows-docker`, apart from native results. Keep the image local; do
not push it.

```bash
docker/build.sh            # builds etf-risk:dev; records the commit and whether src/, pyproject.toml, uv.lock were clean
docker/run.sh              # the test suite in the container (the transcript-hook tests stay native)
# Steps 4-5 in the container, on the definitions from step 3
docker/run.sh python -m etf_risk.spark_pipeline --windows data/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21 \
    --out-root data/outputs-docker/windows --run-id first
docker/run.sh python -m etf_risk.verify --run data/outputs-docker/windows/$SNAPSHOT/rolling-252-s21/first
```

The SQL analyses run natively on a container run's folder as well. The image
has no `.git`, so run records take the commit and clean flag from the build
(`code_source: "build"`) and the image ID from `docker/run.sh`; `source_sha256`
still identifies the code. `docker/run.sh` sets a memory limit
(`ETF_RISK_MEMORY`, default `2.5g`, a budget to validate) with no swap and
prints the container's cgroup memory peak, which includes page cache. Timings
in the container (a Linux VM on macOS, data on bind mounts) are a separate
configuration, not comparable with native measurements.

## Data

Daily prices come from Yahoo Finance through yfinance and are not committed
(`data/` is gitignored; the data's terms of use have not been reviewed). The
run of record uses the full history of NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, TSLA and QQQ through
2025-12-31 (snapshot `full-2026-10-12`); a 2020–2025 snapshot of the four
stocks was used for the prototype. Download settings, dates, checksums, the
checks run, and open limitations are in [docs/data-sources.md](docs/data-sources.md).

**Data status: partially checked, not fully verified.** Trading dates match
the NYSE schedule, and Adj Close is consistent with Yahoo's own dividend
records. For splits, none of the 23 split-day returns resembles an unadjusted
split; this does not independently prove that every split adjustment is
correct. A second-source comparison and a terms-of-use review have not been
done, and 36 extreme price moves, including AAPL on 2000-09-29, are
**unverified**.

## Course concepts

- **Python**: a sequential reference model with hand-calculated tests, and the
  data checks.
- **PyArrow and Parquet**: daily returns, window definitions and results with
  explicit schemas.
- **PySpark and Spark SQL**: grouped pandas functions and a broadcast join over
  every window; DataFrame aggregation and three SQL analyses; execution plans
  read with `explain("formatted")`.
- **Docker**: an image that reproduces the native results exactly on this
  project's machine.
- **Performance measurement**: fresh-process runs with memory sampling and a
  stop rule; a stride experiment whose design and predictions were committed
  before any measured run; a shuffle-partition experiment, likewise committed
  in advance, that compared three partition settings and recorded the
  partition counts Spark used; a pandas baseline, committed the same way, that
  compared the Spark pipeline end to end with a single-process pandas
  implementation; and a caching experiment, committed the same way, that
  compared three caching strategies and checked every cache in Spark's storage
  information and execution plans.

## AI assistance

Most of the code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code (Opus
5.5) in reviewable stages. I set the requirements and constraints of each
stage, made the design decisions (often choosing among options Claude Code
proposed), reviewed results and diffs, and approved each commit. Each file
written or drafted with AI says so in its header (`AI contribution: ...`),
together with how it was checked.

- **Written by me:** the breach branch of `simulate_path()` in
  `src/etf_risk/model.py`, and the SQL queries in `analysis/`. The queries were
  tutored exercises: Claude Code set the tasks and acceptance criteria and
  reviewed my attempts and my reading of the execution plan, without writing
  the queries. It later added the scripts' command-line input.
- **Other tools:** the transcript hook (`.claude/hooks/save_transcript.py`) was
  first drafted with Codex assistance, inspired by a `log_ai.py` script from a
  CS639 project; Claude Code later changed it to save one log per message and
  wrote its redaction module. The 2020–2025 prototype data was downloaded by a
  check written with Codex assistance outside this repository.
- **Records:** `docs/ai-usage/` holds redacted per-message transcripts of the
  Claude Code sessions, which I review before committing them
  ([docs/ai-usage/README.md](docs/ai-usage/README.md)). The hook does not commit
  or push files and has been checked against real sessions; conversations with
  other AI tools are not recorded.

## Next steps

1. **Performance experiments** (mine): the stride, shuffle-partition and
   caching experiments and the pandas baseline are complete
   ([docs/experiments.md](docs/experiments.md),
   [docs/partition-experiment.md](docs/partition-experiment.md),
   [docs/pandas-baseline.md](docs/pandas-baseline.md),
   [docs/caching-experiment.md](docs/caching-experiment.md)).
2. **Data**: compare the 36 unverified extreme days with a second source, and
   review the data's terms of use.
3. **Figures and the final write-up** (Stage 4).
4. **Optional systems extension** (spec §11): Docker Compose with MySQL, Kafka
   and Redis for a job queue and a result cache, with recovery and caching
   experiments.

1	# Leveraged ETF Risk Analytics — specification
2	
3	Last updated 2026-10-22. Implemented: the pipeline, three Spark SQL analyses of
4	its results, a Docker image, the stride experiment
5	([experiments.md](experiments.md)), the shuffle-partition experiment
6	([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)), the pandas baseline
7	([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)) and the caching experiment
8	([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)); planned: an optional systems
9	extension with MySQL, Kafka and Redis (§11).
10	Every section separates what is **implemented** from what is **planned**.
11	Planned parts describe intentions, not results, and may change when each stage
12	is reviewed.
13	
14	| Stage | Scope | Status |
15	|---|---|---|
16	| Prototype | Reference model; Spark run over one full-period path per ticker and leverage; Python/Spark consistency checks; 2020–2025 data | **Implemented** (now expressed as full-period windows) |
17	| Stage 1 | Full-history download, checksum-enforced ingestion, data validation, [data-sources.md](data-sources.md) | **Implemented** |
18	| Stage 2 | Fixed 252-trading-day holding windows, with the Spark grouping keys, 1x/2x pairing, breach end dates and reference check reworked together; a first sparse-stride run with measured runtime and memory | **Implemented**, including the review cleanup; stride-21 run reviewed |
19	| Stage 3 | Spark SQL analysis of the results, a reproducible environment (Docker) and performance experiments | **Implemented**: three SQL analyses, the Docker image, the stride experiment ([experiments.md](experiments.md)), the shuffle-partition experiment ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)), the pandas baseline ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)) and the caching experiment ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)) |
20	| Extension (optional) | Job queue (MySQL job table, Kafka), result cache (Redis), Docker Compose; recovery and caching experiments (§11) | Planned |
21	| Stage 4 | Figures, final documentation and demo | Planned |
22	
23	## 1. Purpose and scope
24	
25	This independent project studies how a fund that resets to a fixed multiple of
26	its underlying every trading day behaves over a holding period: its return
27	compared with the underlying, its drawdowns, and the rebalancing the daily
28	reset implies. It replays the model on historical daily returns of NVDA, AAPL,
29	MSFT, TSLA and QQQ, and uses Spark to run many holding windows in batch.
30	
31	Out of scope: forecasting any real ETF's NAV (fees, financing and execution are
32	ignored), estimating the market impact of rebalancing, and probability
33	statements about future returns. Results describe historical windows of a few
34	tickers.
35	
36	Course concepts applied: a Python reference implementation with tests; Parquet
37	with explicit schemas (PyArrow); PySpark batch processing with grouped pandas
38	functions; Spark DataFrame aggregation and three Spark SQL analyses; performance
39	measurement (a stride experiment, a shuffle-partition experiment and a pandas
40	baseline); a Docker image for the pipeline.
41	An optional systems extension (§11) explores a job queue and a result cache
42	around the pipeline; nothing in the analysis depends on it.
43	
44	## 2. Research questions
45	
46	1. **Path dependence.** Over the same fixed holding period, how does the path of
47	   the underlying's daily returns shape the result of a daily-reset 2x model,
48	   compared with the underlying itself and with twice its return?
49	2. **Rebalancing.** Under the model's assumptions, how large is the exposure
50	   adjustment the daily reset requires, relative to NAV, and how does it depend
51	   on leverage and the day's return? Dollar amounts scale linearly with NAV, so
52	   results are given per unit of NAV; a hypothetical fund size only rescales them.
53	3. **Spark performance.** How do workload size, partitioning and caching affect
54	   Spark runtime and memory for this workload on one machine, and why?
55	
56	Engineering questions for the optional systems extension (job processing,
57	recovery, result caching) are in §11; they concern the infrastructure around
58	the pipeline, not the analysis.
59	
60	## 3. Model — implemented (`src/etf_risk/model.py`)
61	
62	With `r_t` the underlying's simple return on day `t`, `L` the daily target
63	leverage and `V_(t-1)` the NAV at the start of day `t`:
64	
65	```text
66	V_t               = V_(t-1) × (1 + L × r_t)
67	exposure_before_t = L × V_(t-1) × (1 + r_t)     end of day, before the reset
68	exposure_target_t = L × V_t                     after the reset
69	rebalance_t       = exposure_target_t − exposure_before_t = L × (L − 1) × V_(t-1) × r_t
70	```
71	
72	A positive rebalance adds exposure, a negative one cuts it. It is a
73	model-implied amount, not observed trading.
74	
75	**Assumptions**
76	
77	- The fund holds exposure `L × V_(t-1)` during day `t`, does not trade intraday,
78	  and resets to `L × V_t` at the close.
79	- Underlying returns are total returns (computed from Adj Close, so dividends
80	  are reinvested).
81	- No fees, financing costs, interest on cash, creations or redemptions, taxes,
82	  tracking error or trading costs, so the NAV is not a forecast of any real ETF.
83	- `L > 0` (no inverse funds). Every path starts at NAV 100, and NAV carries over
84	  from day to day.
85	- Invalid input raises an error and is never treated as a breach: returns must
86	  be finite and at least −100%, and `L` and the starting NAV must be finite and
87	  positive.
88	
89	**Breach rule.** If `1 + L × r_t ≤ 0`, the NAV would reach zero or go negative,
90	which the model cannot represent. Day `t` is recorded with status `breach`, NaN
91	NAV, NaN target exposure and NaN rebalance, and the path stops; later days are
92	not output, so a breached path is shorter than its input. The path summary
93	reports `breached`, `breach_day`, and NaN `final_nav` and `total_return`;
94	drawdown and rebalance metrics cover the days before the breach. A breach is a
95	model boundary, not a modeled liquidation of a real product. For `L = 2` it
96	requires a daily return of −50% or worse.
97	
98	**Per-day output**: `day, daily_return, nav_start, nav, exposure_before,
99	exposure_target, rebalance, status, running_peak, drawdown`. The running peak
100	includes the starting NAV, and `drawdown_t = 1 − V_t / running_peak_t`.
101	
102	**Path summary** (`summarize_path`): `days_ok, breached, breach_day, final_nav,
103	total_return, max_drawdown, total_abs_rebalance, max_abs_rebalance`.
104	
105	**Normalized rebalancing (implemented in Stage 2, computed in Spark; `model.py`
106	unchanged)**: daily turnover `|rebalance_t| / V_(t-1)`, a fraction of that day's
107	starting NAV and so not biased by NAV growth (model identity `L(L−1)|r_t|`, exactly
108	0 at 1x). Per path, over the days before any breach: mean, maximum (with the
109	earliest date of the maximum) and total turnover, each stored with its day
110	count. Per window, from the returns alone: realized variance `Σ r_t²` and the
111	exact gap `Σ log(1 − (r_t/(1+r_t))²)`, both null unless every term is valid.
112	Dollar rebalance sums stay only for the reference comparison.
113	
114	## 4. Data inputs and outputs
115	
116	### Implemented
117	
118	| Artifact | Location (gitignored) | Produced by | Contents |
119	|---|---|---|---|
120	| Raw snapshot | `data/raw/yahoo/<snapshot>/` | `download.py` | one CSV per ticker (Date, Open, High, Low, Close, Adj Close, Volume, Dividends, Stock Splits; QQQ also has Capital Gains, all zero in `full-2026-10-12` and unused) and `manifest.json` (download time, tool versions, request settings, rows, dates, SHA-256 per file); the prototype snapshot sits in `data/raw/yahoo/` with `verification.json` |
121	| Daily returns | `data/processed/<snapshot>/daily_returns/<TICKER>.parquet` | `ingest.py` | `ticker` string, `date` date32, `adjusted_price` double, `daily_return` double (null on the first row); schema metadata naming the source, snapshot and checksums |
122	| Quality report | `data/processed/<snapshot>/quality_report.json` | `ingest.py` | per-ticker check results, a verification-status block, and the list of unverified extreme days |
123	| Window definitions | `data/windows/<snapshot>/<name>/` (`windows.parquet`, `config.json`) | `windows.py` | one row per window: `window_kind, ticker, window_days, entry_date, first_return_date, exit_date, entry_row, stride, calendar_year, contains_unverified_day, unverified_day_count, entry_on_unverified_day`; the config records the SHA-256 of every return file, of `quality_report.json` and of `windows.parquet`, the self-check results, the flag rule, each return file's raw-manifest hash, and the code that built it (commit, whether the worktree was clean, SHA-256 of every source file and of `uv.lock`) |
124	| Run output | `data/outputs/windows/<snapshot>/<name>/<run id>/` | `spark_pipeline.py`, `verify.py` | `window_stats/` (one row per window, no model), `path_days/` (per window, leverage and day; partitioned by ticker), `path_summary/` (per window and leverage), `paired/` (per window, 1x and 2x; for a breached 2x path the full-window 2x drawdown and turnover columns are null and the partial values sit in `*_pre_breach` columns with `days_ok_2x`), `checks.json`, `run.json` (including the code provenance and the JVM's measured maximum heap), and `verify.json` from the sample check |
125	| Measurement records | `data/outputs/windows/<snapshot>/<name>/protocol-<UTC time>.json`, `<run id>.log` (the stride experiment: under `data/outputs-experiments/`) | `measure.py` | per run: wall time, in-process phase timings, peak summed RSS in total and per process type, stop-rule status and its limits |
126	| Measurements CSV | `data/outputs-experiments/measurements.csv` | `analysis/collect_measurements.py` | one row per started run of the stride experiment: identity and role, input size, Spark settings, summed stage task counts, wall and phase times, peak RSS by process type, sampling, code ([experiments.md](experiments.md) 5.6) |
127	| Execution plans | `plans.json` in a run folder | `spark_pipeline.py --record-plans` (`plans.py`) | for every SQL execution of the run: its phase and final plan text, each shuffle exchange's requested and runtime partition counts, each AQE shuffle read's mark and partition count ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md) 4.2); in format 2, also each execution's description and scan nodes ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md) 4.2) |

129	| Pandas-baseline batch | `data/outputs-baseline/<batch>/` | `measure.py --pipeline` through `docs/baseline-session.zsh`; `analysis/collect_baseline_measurements.py` | protocols and runs of S (the Spark pipeline) and P (the pandas pipeline), `positions.tsv`, `run-log.txt`, and the collector's `measurements.csv` and `acceptance.json` ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md) 2.4, 4.3) |

# Leveraged ETF Risk Analytics — specification

Last updated 2026-10-22. Implemented: the pipeline, three Spark SQL analyses of
its results, a Docker image, the stride experiment
([experiments.md](experiments.md)), the shuffle-partition experiment
([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)), the pandas baseline
([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)) and the caching experiment
([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)); planned: an optional systems
extension with MySQL, Kafka and Redis (§11).
Every section separates what is **implemented** from what is **planned**.
Planned parts describe intentions, not results, and may change when each stage
is reviewed.

| Stage | Scope | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Prototype | Reference model; Spark run over one full-period path per ticker and leverage; Python/Spark consistency checks; 2020–2025 data | **Implemented** (now expressed as full-period windows) |
| Stage 1 | Full-history download, checksum-enforced ingestion, data validation, [data-sources.md](data-sources.md) | **Implemented** |
| Stage 2 | Fixed 252-trading-day holding windows, with the Spark grouping keys, 1x/2x pairing, breach end dates and reference check reworked together; a first sparse-stride run with measured runtime and memory | **Implemented**, including the review cleanup; stride-21 run reviewed |
| Stage 3 | Spark SQL analysis of the results, a reproducible environment (Docker) and performance experiments | **Implemented**: three SQL analyses, the Docker image, the stride experiment ([experiments.md](experiments.md)), the shuffle-partition experiment ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)), the pandas baseline ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)) and the caching experiment ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)) |
| Extension (optional) | Job queue (MySQL job table, Kafka), result cache (Redis), Docker Compose; recovery and caching experiments (§11) | Planned |
| Stage 4 | Figures, final documentation and demo | Planned |

## 1. Purpose and scope

This independent project studies how a fund that resets to a fixed multiple of
its underlying every trading day behaves over a holding period: its return
compared with the underlying, its drawdowns, and the rebalancing the daily
reset implies. It replays the model on historical daily returns of NVDA, AAPL,
MSFT, TSLA and QQQ, and uses Spark to run many holding windows in batch.

Out of scope: forecasting any real ETF's NAV (fees, financing and execution are
ignored), estimating the market impact of rebalancing, and probability
statements about future returns. Results describe historical windows of a few
tickers.

Course concepts applied: a Python reference implementation with tests; Parquet
with explicit schemas (PyArrow); PySpark batch processing with grouped pandas
functions; Spark DataFrame aggregation and three Spark SQL analyses; performance
measurement (a stride experiment, a shuffle-partition experiment and a pandas
baseline); a Docker image for the pipeline.
An optional systems extension (§11) explores a job queue and a result cache
around the pipeline; nothing in the analysis depends on it.

## 2. Research questions

1. **Path dependence.** Over the same fixed holding period, how does the path of
   the underlying's daily returns shape the result of a daily-reset 2x model,
   compared with the underlying itself and with twice its return?
2. **Rebalancing.** Under the model's assumptions, how large is the exposure
   adjustment the daily reset requires, relative to NAV, and how does it depend
   on leverage and the day's return? Dollar amounts scale linearly with NAV, so
   results are given per unit of NAV; a hypothetical fund size only rescales them.
3. **Spark performance.** How do workload size, partitioning and caching affect
   Spark runtime and memory for this workload on one machine, and why?

Engineering questions for the optional systems extension (job processing,
recovery, result caching) are in §11; they concern the infrastructure around
the pipeline, not the analysis.

## 3. Model — implemented (`src/etf_risk/model.py`)

With `r_t` the underlying's simple return on day `t`, `L` the daily target
leverage and `V_(t-1)` the NAV at the start of day `t`:

```text
V_t               = V_(t-1) × (1 + L × r_t)
exposure_before_t = L × V_(t-1) × (1 + r_t)     end of day, before the reset
exposure_target_t = L × V_t                     after the reset
rebalance_t       = exposure_target_t − exposure_before_t = L × (L − 1) × V_(t-1) × r_t
```

A positive rebalance adds exposure, a negative one cuts it. It is a
model-implied amount, not observed trading.

**Assumptions**

- The fund holds exposure `L × V_(t-1)` during day `t`, does not trade intraday,
  and resets to `L × V_t` at the close.
- Underlying returns are total returns (computed from Adj Close, so dividends
  are reinvested).
- No fees, financing costs, interest on cash, creations or redemptions, taxes,
  tracking error or trading costs, so the NAV is not a forecast of any real ETF.
- `L > 0` (no inverse funds). Every path starts at NAV 100, and NAV carries over
  from day to day.
- Invalid input raises an error and is never treated as a breach: returns must
  be finite and at least −100%, and `L` and the starting NAV must be finite and
  positive.

**Breach rule.** If `1 + L × r_t ≤ 0`, the NAV would reach zero or go negative,
which the model cannot represent. Day `t` is recorded with status `breach`, NaN
NAV, NaN target exposure and NaN rebalance, and the path stops; later days are
not output, so a breached path is shorter than its input. The path summary
reports `breached`, `breach_day`, and NaN `final_nav` and `total_return`;
drawdown and rebalance metrics cover the days before the breach. A breach is a
model boundary, not a modeled liquidation of a real product. For `L = 2` it
requires a daily return of −50% or worse.

**Per-day output**: `day, daily_return, nav_start, nav, exposure_before,
exposure_target, rebalance, status, running_peak, drawdown`. The running peak
includes the starting NAV, and `drawdown_t = 1 − V_t / running_peak_t`.

**Path summary** (`summarize_path`): `days_ok, breached, breach_day, final_nav,
total_return, max_drawdown, total_abs_rebalance, max_abs_rebalance`.

**Normalized rebalancing (implemented in Stage 2, computed in Spark; `model.py`
unchanged)**: daily turnover `|rebalance_t| / V_(t-1)`, a fraction of that day's
starting NAV and so not biased by NAV growth (model identity `L(L−1)|r_t|`, exactly
0 at 1x). Per path, over the days before any breach: mean, maximum (with the
earliest date of the maximum) and total turnover, each stored with its day
count. Per window, from the returns alone: realized variance `Σ r_t²` and the
exact gap `Σ log(1 − (r_t/(1+r_t))²)`, both null unless every term is valid.
Dollar rebalance sums stay only for the reference comparison.

## 4. Data inputs and outputs

### Implemented

| Daily returns | `data/processed/<snapshot>/daily_returns/<TICKER>.parquet` | `ingest.py` | `ticker` string, `date` date32, `adjusted_price` double, `daily_return` double (null on the first row); schema metadata naming the source, snapshot and checksums |

| Window definitions | `data/windows/<snapshot>/<name>/` (`windows.parquet`, `config.json`) | `windows.py` | one row per window: `window_kind, ticker, window_days, entry_date, first_return_date, exit_date, entry_row, stride, calendar_year, contains_unverified_day, unverified_day_count, entry_on_unverified_day`; the config records the SHA-256 of every return file, of `quality_report.json` and of `windows.parquet`, the self-check results, the flag rule, each return file's raw-manifest hash, and the code that built it (commit, whether the worktree was clean, SHA-256 of every source file and of `uv.lock`) |

369	## 8. Expected results
370	
371	These are expectations derived from the model, written down before the Stage 2
372	runs so the results can be checked against them rather than fitted afterwards.
373	
374	1. **Path dependence (question 1).** Each day, `(1 + r)² − (1 + 2r) = r²`, so for
375	   a 2x window without a breach the log-return gap is exactly
376	
377	   ```text
378	   log(1 + R_2x) − 2 × log(1 + R_1x) = Σ log(1 − (r_t / (1 + r_t))²)  ≤ 0
379	                                      ≈ −Σ r_t²   (realized variance; error of order Σ r_t³)
380	   ```
381	
382	   In log terms the 2x model always falls short of twice the underlying, by about
383	   the window's realized variance. In simple returns it can still beat twice the
384	   underlying's return in strong, steady trends, because compounding adds
385	   `R_1x²`, and it falls short in volatile windows without a trend. Checked so
386	   far only outside the pipeline, on the 2020–2025 prototype data: the exact
387	   identity matches the model output to about 1e−15 on all four full-period
388	   paths, and the approximation is within 5% of the exact gap in 18 of 20
389	   non-overlapping 252-day blocks; the largest difference, 13.8% for NVDA in
390	   2023, comes from a block with a +24.4% day.
391	2. **Drawdowns.** Each day `1 + L r ≤ (1 + r)^L` for `L ≥ 1` (Bernoulli's
392	   inequality). Over the interval from the 1x path's peak to its trough, the
393	   leveraged NAV therefore ends at no more than `(1 − MDD_1x)^L` times its value
394	   at the start of that interval. For every window without a breach,
395	   `MDD_2x ≥ 1 − (1 − MDD_1x)²`: a 30% drawdown at 1x implies at least 51% at 2x.
396	   The four prototype paths satisfy this (NVDA: 1x 66.3%, bound 88.7%, 2x 92.1%).
397	3. **Breaches.** At 2x only a day of −50% or worse causes a breach. In
398	   `full-2026-10-12` the only such day is AAPL 2000-09-29 (−51.9%, unverified),
399	   so breached 2x windows are expected only among AAPL windows that include it,
400	   and every result about them will be labeled unverified.
401	4. **Rebalancing (question 2).** Under the model, the rebalance as a fraction of
402	   that day's starting NAV is exactly `L(L − 1) r_t`: for 2x, twice the day's
403	   return, adding exposure after up days and cutting it after down days. Daily
404	   turnover is therefore `2 |r_t|`, and its distribution per ticker is that of
405	   `|r_t|` rescaled. The results will report magnitudes, not market impact. The
406	   largest values fall on extreme days, which are unverified.
407	5. **Spark performance (question 3).** These are hypotheses to test, not
408	   findings. At sparse strides, fixed costs (starting the Spark session and the
409	   Python workers) should dominate. Larger workloads should take longer roughly
410	   in proportion to the number of windows. Expanding returns into windows
411	   multiplies the rows Spark has to shuffle by about `252 / stride`, and running
412	   one grouped pandas call per window adds a per-window Python cost. Spark's
413	   adaptive execution may merge shuffle partitions, so requested and actual
414	   partition counts will both be recorded. A single-process pandas run may be
415	   faster at these sizes. Memory will be measured, not estimated. At the time
416	   these expectations were recorded, the only timing available was an informal
417	   prototype run. The subsequent measurements and their limitations are
418	   reported below.
419	
420	### What the stride-21 run showed (`full-2026-10-12`, after the cleanup)
421	
422	Descriptive facts from one configuration, not findings about markets. The rolling
423	windows overlap. Run of record: `rolling-252-s21-r2`, protocol
424	`20261013T043848Z` (code with uncommitted changes, identified by its source
425	checksums in every record).
426	
427	- **Checks.** All 46 check tests (ten checks) passed with no violation on 1,790
428	  windows, so the exact log-gap identity (expectation 1) and the drawdown bound
429	  (expectation 2) held in every one of the 1,778 windows without a breach. These
430	  identities test the model against the same member rows; window dates rest on
431	  check 1, the definition self-check (no violation) and `verify.py`. The sample
432	  check compared 1,074 paths in 537 windows with no mismatch, and Python and Spark
433	  found the same 12 breached windows. The calendar-year supplement (151 windows)
434	  and the full-period regression on the prototype snapshot also passed; the
435	  regression reproduced the prototype's results exactly.
436	- **Breaches (expectation 3).** Exactly 12 rolling windows breach at 2x, all AAPL
437	  windows containing 2000-09-29, plus the calendar year AAPL 2000; all are
438	  flagged unverified and listed separately with their pre-breach values.
439	- **Approximation.** Over each ticker's windows without a breach (flagged windows
440	  included), the median relative error of `−Σr²` against the exact gap lies
441	  between −1.2% (NVDA) and +0.3% (TSLA), with interquartile ranges between −4.3%
442	  and +2.5%.
443	- **Turnover (expectation 4).** The median of the 2x mean daily turnover per
444	  window ranges from 1.8% of NAV (QQQ) to 5.0% (TSLA); breached windows excluded.
445	- **Sensitivity to unverified days.** Leaving out the 239 flagged windows moves
446	  some medians noticeably (TSLA 2x return +13.5% across all 174 windows, −12.3%
447	  across the 117 unflagged ones). This shows how much results depend on periods
448	  with extreme market days; it is not evidence that those days are data errors.
449	- **Runtime and memory (expectation 5).** Measured on one machine and
450	  configuration only: an Apple Silicon laptop (8 cores, 8 GiB RAM), Spark in
451	  local mode with default settings; other machines and settings have not been
452	  measured. 900,714 path-day rows from 451,080 window-member rows. Over three
453	  measured fresh-process runs after one warm-up:
454	  median wall time 44.7 s (40.2–47.0 s), of which Spark start-up took about 4 s,
455	  the model and `path_days` write 12–16 s, and summaries and pairing 10–12 s;
456	  median peak summed RSS 1.27 GiB (1.24–1.45 GiB) against a 4.8 GiB stop threshold,
457	  which no run reached; the driver JVM's measured maximum heap was 1.0 GiB. Only
458	  1.3–1.6 GiB of memory was free before each run. Sampling every 0.25 s can miss
459	  shorter peaks, summed RSS can overstate shared pages, per-process-type peaks
460	  occur at different moments, and the 60% threshold is an experimental limit
461	  for this machine, not a measured safe bound. Adaptive execution was on with
462	  Spark's defaults (200 shuffle partitions, partition merging enabled). The
463	  stride experiment below varied only the workload; the shuffle-partition
464	  experiment compared these defaults with two other settings at stride 7.
465	
466	### Spark SQL analyses of the run of record
467	
468	Three scripts in `analysis/`, written by the project author, query the run's
469	`paired` table; each takes the run folder as its argument (README, step 6).
470	Every statistic is reported with the number of windows it covers. Ticker order:
471	AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, TSLA, then QQQ.
472	
473	- **`sql_overview.py`**: windows 529, 466, 311, 174, 310; 2x breaches 12 (AAPL)
474	  and none elsewhere; windows using an unverified day 78, 12, 92, 57, 0. Exact
475	  median 1x return 24.4%, 22.8%, 39.5%, 22.5%, 16.6%; median 2x return 35.2%
476	  (over AAPL's 517 windows with a 2x return), 39.9%, 51.3%, 13.5%, 31.4%.
477	- **`sql_comparison.py`**: the 2x return exceeded twice the 1x return in 219 of
478	  AAPL's 517 windows with both returns (42.4%), 164 of 466 (35.2%), 141 of 311
479	  (45.3%), 43 of 174 (24.7%) and 140 of 310 (45.2%). The 12 breached windows are
480	  counted as not compared, not as failures.
481	- **`sql_sensitivity.py`**: without the windows that use an unverified day, the
482	  median 2x return is 48.5% (AAPL, 451 windows), 41.4% (454), 52.2% (219) and
483	  −12.3% (TSLA, 117); QQQ has no such windows (31.4%, 310). As above, this is a
484	  sensitivity analysis, not evidence of data errors.
485	
486	### What the stride experiment showed (2026-10-19)
487	
488	Measured on the same machine and with the same Spark settings as the run of
489	record, varying only the workload; the design and predictions were committed
490	before any measured run. Design, run log, records and answers:
491	[experiments.md](experiments.md).
492	
493	- **Runs.** Five protocols of four fresh-process runs (one warm-up, three
494	  measured): strides 21, 14 and 7 as planned, stride 3, and stride 21 again
495	  as a drift check. All 20 runs passed every check, and no sample reached the
496	  4.8 GiB stop threshold.
497	- **Stride 3 is exploratory.** The experiment's rule for admitting stride 3
498	  failed on projected memory; the author ran it anyway, to see whether it
499	  would complete. Its results (median wall time 40.2 s, median peak 2.73 GiB)
500	  are reported separately, never as a planned point.
501	- **Drift.** The repeated stride-21 median (18.2 s) was 18.3% below the first
502	  (22.2 s), outside the 10% tolerance, so comparisons across strides are
503	  marked as affected. Which apps were open during the last two protocols is
504	  uncertain.
505	- **Expectation 5.** Median wall times were 22.2, 20.3 and 25.7 s at strides
506	  21, 14 and 7, for 1, 1.5 and 3 times the windows. A linear fit over these
507	  three medians gives an intercept of 18.8 s (85% of the stride-21 median) and
508	  1.2 ms per window, with every fitted value within 8.5% of its median. This
509	  meets the experiment's numerical criteria for fixed costs dominating at
510	  stride 21 and for roughly linear growth, but three points and the drift make
511	  the evidence weak, and the intercept is an estimate, not measured overhead:
512	  the timed fixed parts (Spark start-up and the time outside the pipeline's
513	  clock) took 4.4 s. The model phase grew 1.66 times while the windows grew 3
514	  times. Median peak memory rose only from 2.62 to 2.70 GiB; the driver JVM's
515	  resident memory exceeded its 1.0 GiB heap by 0.52 to 0.57 GiB.
516	- **Against the run of record.** At stride 21 the median wall time was half
517	  the run of record's (22.2 against 44.7 s) and the median peak about twice
518	  (2.62 against 1.27 GiB), with 3.0–3.5 instead of 1.3–1.6 GiB free before
519	  the runs. The code (apart from `provenance.py`), the windows and the Spark
520	  settings were the same; the records cannot establish the cause.
521	- **Not measured.** The shuffle partition counts Spark actually used (only the
522	  200 requested and the summed stage task counts per phase were recorded),
523	  spilling and CPU use; the single-process pandas comparison was not run. The
524	  shuffle-partition experiment, below, recorded the actual partition counts of
525	  its own runs ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md) 4.2, 14.8),
526	  and the pandas baseline, below, ran the pandas comparison
527	  ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)).
528	
529	### What the shuffle-partition experiment showed (2026-10-22)
530	
531	Measured on the same machine with the stride experiment's stride-7 workload,
532	varying only three Spark settings; the design, code and predictions were
533	committed before any measured run. Design, run log, records and answers:
534	[partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md).
535	
536	- **Settings.** A: Spark's defaults, set explicitly (200 shuffle partitions,
537	  AQE coalescing on); B: 200 partitions, coalescing off; C: 8 partitions (one
538	  per core), coalescing off. AQE stayed enabled in all three.
539	- **Runs.** Six protocols of four fresh-process runs (one warm-up, three
540	  measured) in the order A–B–C–C–B–A, in one batch. All 24 runs passed every
541	  check, no sample reached the 4.8 GiB stop threshold, and the batch met every
542	  acceptance criterion: one code state, unchanged inputs, settings verified in
543	  the recorded configuration and the execution plans, and outputs matching A's.
544	- **Time.** Median times without the plan recording were 26.5 s (A), 44.6 s
545	  (B) and 25.3 s (C). B's median was 69% longer than A's and 77% longer than
546	  C's, in the same direction in both halves of the order. A's was 1.18 s above
547	  C's, below the experiment's threshold of 10% of A's median, so A and C show
548	  no clear difference. B's extra time over A fell mostly in the summaries
549	  (7.6 s), the window statistics (5.5 s) and the model phase (4.0 s).
550	- **Plans.** In A, AQE coalesced ten shuffle reads to 1 to 9 partitions; in B,
551	  every read used all 200. B's summed stage task counts were 3.3 to 19.7 times
552	  A's, and it wrote 1,584 output files against A's 50. In B, the join behind

559	  in the last bits of 12 floating-point columns (at most 2.1e-14 in `paired`

561	- **Predictions.** All three median times and peaks were inside their
562	  predicted ranges, and the predicted comparisons held. B's median was 35%
563	  above its predicted 33 s; the prediction left out the sort-merge join, and
564	  the records cannot separate the costs of the mechanisms.
565	- **Conditions.** No drift was detected: A's two protocols, three hours apart,
566	  differed by 0.9%. The machine checks were recorded only before the first
567	  protocol, and the last protocol followed a two-hour break. CPU time,
568	  spilling and GC were not measured.

621	- **Time.** Median times without the plan recording were 26.5 s (A), 27.0 s

623	  were slower in each half. Both differences were below the threshold of 10%

## 8. Expected results

These are expectations derived from the model, written down before the Stage 2
runs so the results can be checked against them rather than fitted afterwards.

1. **Path dependence (question 1).** Each day, `(1 + r)² − (1 + 2r) = r²`, so for
   a 2x window without a breach the log-return gap is exactly

   ```text
   log(1 + R_2x) − 2 × log(1 + R_1x) = Σ log(1 − (r_t / (1 + r_t))²)  ≤ 0
                                      ≈ −Σ r_t²   (realized variance; error of order Σ r_t³)
   ```

   In log terms the 2x model always falls short of twice the underlying, by about
   the window's realized variance. In simple returns it can still beat twice the
   underlying's return in strong, steady trends, because compounding adds
   `R_1x²`, and it falls short in volatile windows without a trend. Checked so
   far only outside the pipeline, on the 2020–2025 prototype data: the exact
   identity matches the model output to about 1e−15 on all four full-period
   paths, and the approximation is within 5% of the exact gap in 18 of 20
   non-overlapping 252-day blocks; the largest difference, 13.8% for NVDA in
   2023, comes from a block with a +24.4% day.
2. **Drawdowns.** Each day `1 + L r ≤ (1 + r)^L` for `L ≥ 1` (Bernoulli's
   inequality). Over the interval from the 1x path's peak to its trough, the
   leveraged NAV therefore ends at no more than `(1 − MDD_1x)^L` times its value
   at the start of that interval. For every window without a breach,
   `MDD_2x ≥ 1 − (1 − MDD_1x)²`: a 30% drawdown at 1x implies at least 51% at 2x.
   The four prototype paths satisfy this (NVDA: 1x 66.3%, bound 88.7%, 2x 92.1%).
3. **Breaches.** At 2x only a day of −50% or worse causes a breach. In
   `full-2026-10-12` the only such day is AAPL 2000-09-29 (−51.9%, unverified),
   so breached 2x windows are expected only among AAPL windows that include it,
   and every result about them will be labeled unverified.
4. **Rebalancing (question 2).** Under the model, the rebalance as a fraction of
   that day's starting NAV is exactly `L(L − 1) r_t`: for 2x, twice the day's
   return, adding exposure after up days and cutting it after down days. Daily
   turnover is therefore `2 |r_t|`, and its distribution per ticker is that of
   `|r_t|` rescaled. The results will report magnitudes, not market impact. The
   largest values fall on extreme days, which are unverified.
5. **Spark performance (question 3).** These are hypotheses to test, not
   findings. At sparse strides, fixed costs (starting the Spark session and the
   Python workers) should dominate. Larger workloads should take longer roughly
   in proportion to the number of windows. Expanding returns into windows
   multiplies the rows Spark has to shuffle by about `252 / stride`, and running
   one grouped pandas call per window adds a per-window Python cost. Spark's
   adaptive execution may merge shuffle partitions, so requested and actual
   partition counts will both be recorded. A single-process pandas run may be
   faster at these sizes. Memory will be measured, not estimated. At the time
   these expectations were recorded, the only timing available was an informal
   prototype run. The subsequent measurements and their limitations are
   reported below.

### What the stride-21 run showed (`full-2026-10-12`, after the cleanup)

Descriptive facts from one configuration, not findings about markets. The rolling
windows overlap. Run of record: `rolling-252-s21-r2`, protocol
`20261013T043848Z` (code with uncommitted changes, identified by its source
checksums in every record).

- **Checks.** All 46 check tests (ten checks) passed with no violation on 1,790
  windows, so the exact log-gap identity (expectation 1) and the drawdown bound
  (expectation 2) held in every one of the 1,778 windows without a breach. These
  identities test the model against the same member rows; window dates rest on
  check 1, the definition self-check (no violation) and `verify.py`. The sample
  check compared 1,074 paths in 537 windows with no mismatch, and Python and Spark
  found the same 12 breached windows. The calendar-year supplement (151 windows)
  and the full-period regression on the prototype snapshot also passed; the
  regression reproduced the prototype's results exactly.
- **Breaches (expectation 3).** Exactly 12 rolling windows breach at 2x, all AAPL
  windows containing 2000-09-29, plus the calendar year AAPL 2000; all are
  flagged unverified and listed separately with their pre-breach values.
- **Approximation.** Over each ticker's windows without a breach (flagged windows
  included), the median relative error of `−Σr²` against the exact gap lies
  between −1.2% (NVDA) and +0.3% (TSLA), with interquartile ranges between −4.3%
  and +2.5%.
- **Turnover (expectation 4).** The median of the 2x mean daily turnover per
  window ranges from 1.8% of NAV (QQQ) to 5.0% (TSLA); breached windows excluded.
- **Sensitivity to unverified days.** Leaving out the 239 flagged windows moves
  some medians noticeably (TSLA 2x return +13.5% across all 174 windows, −12.3%
  across the 117 unflagged ones). This shows how much results depend on periods
  with extreme market days; it is not evidence that those days are data errors.
- **Runtime and memory (expectation 5).** Measured on one machine and
  configuration only: an Apple Silicon laptop (8 cores, 8 GiB RAM), Spark in
  local mode with default settings; other machines and settings have not been
  measured. 900,714 path-day rows from 451,080 window-member rows. Over three
  measured fresh-process runs after one warm-up:
  median wall time 44.7 s (40.2–47.0 s), of which Spark start-up took about 4 s,
  the model and `path_days` write 12–16 s, and summaries and pairing 10–12 s;
  median peak summed RSS 1.27 GiB (1.24–1.45 GiB) against a 4.8 GiB stop threshold,
  which no run reached; the driver JVM's measured maximum heap was 1.0 GiB. Only
  1.3–1.6 GiB of memory was free before each run. Sampling every 0.25 s can miss
  shorter peaks, summed RSS can overstate shared pages, per-process-type peaks
  occur at different moments, and the 60% threshold is an experimental limit
  for this machine, not a measured safe bound. Adaptive execution was on with
  Spark's defaults (200 shuffle partitions, partition merging enabled). The
  stride experiment below varied only the workload; the shuffle-partition
  experiment compared these defaults with two other settings at stride 7.

### Spark SQL analyses of the run of record

Three scripts in `analysis/`, written by the project author, query the run's
`paired` table; each takes the run folder as its argument (README, step 6).
Every statistic is reported with the number of windows it covers. Ticker order:
AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, TSLA, then QQQ.

- **`sql_overview.py`**: windows 529, 466, 311, 174, 310; 2x breaches 12 (AAPL)
  and none elsewhere; windows using an unverified day 78, 12, 92, 57, 0. Exact
  median 1x return 24.4%, 22.8%, 39.5%, 22.5%, 16.6%; median 2x return 35.2%
  (over AAPL's 517 windows with a 2x return), 39.9%, 51.3%, 13.5%, 31.4%.
- **`sql_comparison.py`**: the 2x return exceeded twice the 1x return in 219 of
  AAPL's 517 windows with both returns (42.4%), 164 of 466 (35.2%), 141 of 311
  (45.3%), 43 of 174 (24.7%) and 140 of 310 (45.2%). The 12 breached windows are
  counted as not compared, not as failures.
- **`sql_sensitivity.py`**: without the windows that use an unverified day, the
  median 2x return is 48.5% (AAPL, 451 windows), 41.4% (454), 52.2% (219) and
  −12.3% (TSLA, 117); QQQ has no such windows (31.4%, 310). As above, this is a
  sensitivity analysis, not evidence of data errors.

### What the stride experiment showed (2026-10-19)

Measured on the same machine and with the same Spark settings as the run of
record, varying only the workload; the design and predictions were committed
before any measured run. Design, run log, records and answers:
[experiments.md](experiments.md).

- **Runs.** Five protocols of four fresh-process runs (one warm-up, three
  measured): strides 21, 14 and 7 as planned, stride 3, and stride 21 again
  as a drift check. All 20 runs passed every check, and no sample reached the
  4.8 GiB stop threshold.
- **Stride 3 is exploratory.** The experiment's rule for admitting stride 3
  failed on projected memory; the author ran it anyway, to see whether it
  would complete. Its results (median wall time 40.2 s, median peak 2.73 GiB)
  are reported separately, never as a planned point.
- **Drift.** The repeated stride-21 median (18.2 s) was 18.3% below the first
  (22.2 s), outside the 10% tolerance, so comparisons across strides are
  marked as affected. Which apps were open during the last two protocols is
  uncertain.
- **Expectation 5.** Median wall times were 22.2, 20.3 and 25.7 s at strides
  21, 14 and 7, for 1, 1.5 and 3 times the windows. A linear fit over these
  three medians gives an intercept of 18.8 s (85% of the stride-21 median) and
  1.2 ms per window, with every fitted value within 8.5% of its median. This
  meets the experiment's numerical criteria for fixed costs dominating at
  stride 21 and for roughly linear growth, but three points and the drift make
  the evidence weak, and the intercept is an estimate, not measured overhead:
  the timed fixed parts (Spark start-up and the time outside the pipeline's
  clock) took 4.4 s. The model phase grew 1.66 times while the windows grew 3
  times. Median peak memory rose only from 2.62 to 2.70 GiB; the driver JVM's
  resident memory exceeded its 1.0 GiB heap by 0.52 to 0.57 GiB.
- **Against the run of record.** At stride 21 the median wall time was half
  the run of record's (22.2 against 44.7 s) and the median peak about twice
  (2.62 against 1.27 GiB), with 3.0–3.5 instead of 1.3–1.6 GiB free before
  the runs. The code (apart from `provenance.py`), the windows and the Spark
  settings were the same; the records cannot establish the cause.
- **Not measured.** The shuffle partition counts Spark actually used (only the
  200 requested and the summed stage task counts per phase were recorded),
  spilling and CPU use; the single-process pandas comparison was not run. The
  shuffle-partition experiment, below, recorded the actual partition counts of
  its own runs ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md) 4.2, 14.8),
  and the pandas baseline, below, ran the pandas comparison
  ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)).

### What the shuffle-partition experiment showed (2026-10-22)

Measured on the same machine with the stride experiment's stride-7 workload,
varying only three Spark settings; the design, code and predictions were
committed before any measured run. Design, run log, records and answers:
[partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md).

- **Settings.** A: Spark's defaults, set explicitly (200 shuffle partitions,
  AQE coalescing on); B: 200 partitions, coalescing off; C: 8 partitions (one
  per core), coalescing off. AQE stayed enabled in all three.
- **Runs.** Six protocols of four fresh-process runs (one warm-up, three
  measured) in the order A–B–C–C–B–A, in one batch. All 24 runs passed every
  check, no sample reached the 4.8 GiB stop threshold, and the batch met every
  acceptance criterion: one code state, unchanged inputs, settings verified in
  the recorded configuration and the execution plans, and outputs matching A's.
- **Time.** Median times without the plan recording were 26.5 s (A), 44.6 s
  (B) and 25.3 s (C). B's median was 69% longer than A's and 77% longer than
  C's, in the same direction in both halves of the order. A's was 1.18 s above
  C's, below the experiment's threshold of 10% of A's median, so A and C show
  no clear difference. B's extra time over A fell mostly in the summaries
  (7.6 s), the window statistics (5.5 s) and the model phase (4.0 s).
- **Plans.** In A, AQE coalesced ten shuffle reads to 1 to 9 partitions; in B,
  every read used all 200. B's summed stage task counts were 3.3 to 19.7 times
  A's, and it wrote 1,584 output files against A's 50. In B, the join behind
  the window statistics stayed a sort-merge join: the shuffle feeding its
  aggregate side wrote 99.9 MiB, above the recorded 10 MiB broadcast threshold,
  against 6.3 MiB in A and 5.6 MiB in C, where AQE chose a broadcast join.
- **Memory and results.** Median peaks were 2.69 GiB in all three settings,
  with no clear difference. `paired` and `path_summary` matched A's in every
  run: A's runs exactly, and B's and C's within the tolerance, differing only
  in the last bits of 12 floating-point columns (at most 2.1e-14 in `paired`
  and 1.8e-11 in `path_summary`).
- **Predictions.** All three median times and peaks were inside their
  predicted ranges, and the predicted comparisons held. B's median was 35%
  above its predicted 33 s; the prediction left out the sort-merge join, and
  the records cannot separate the costs of the mechanisms.
- **Conditions.** No drift was detected: A's two protocols, three hours apart,
  differed by 0.9%. The machine checks were recorded only before the first
  protocol, and the last protocol followed a two-hour break. CPU time,
  spilling and GC were not measured.

### What the pandas baseline showed (2026-10-22)

Measured on the same machine with the stride-7 workload: an end-to-end
comparison of the Spark pipeline at Spark's defaults (S) with a single-process
pandas implementation of the same computation (P). The design, code and
predictions were committed before any measured run. Design, run log, records
and answers: [pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md).

- **What is compared.** Both implementations call the same model function for
  each window and produce the same tables and checks, but they build the member
  rows, aggregate, check and write in their own ways, and P runs in one process.
  The comparison does not isolate Spark's overhead.
- **Runs.** Four protocols of four fresh-process runs in the order S–P–P–S, in
  one batch. All 16 runs passed every check, no sample reached the 4.8 GiB
  stop threshold, and the batch met every acceptance criterion. The machine
  checks were recorded at every start, and no drift was detected (S +0.97%,
  P +1.17%).
- **Time.** Median wall times were 26.4 s (S) and 15.4 s (P): P's was 41.8%
  shorter, in the same direction in both halves of the order. P's model phase
  took longer than S's (12.1 against 8.6 s), each of its other phases took
  less time, and P has no Spark session start (2.4 s in S).
- **Memory and results.** Median peak total RSS was 2.68 GiB (S) and 1.97 GiB
  (P). Overall, P's median peak total RSS was 26.6% lower; it was lower in both
  halves. P's outputs matched S's within the tolerance, and `path_days`,
  compared in full for two P runs, was identical.
- **Predictions.** S's median time and peak were inside their predicted
  ranges. P's median wall time was below its predicted band (28–60 s) and its
  median peak above its range (0.8–1.8 GiB): the predicted time ranking was
  reversed, while the memory ranking held. For this workload the
  single-process pandas implementation was faster end to end, as the last
  hypothesis of expectation 5 allowed; other sizes were not measured.

### What the caching experiment showed (2026-10-22)

Measured on the same machine with the stride-7 workload, varying only what
Spark caches; the design, code and predictions were committed before any
measured run. Design, run log, records and answers:
[caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md).

- **Configurations.** A: no cache; B: the window-member rows, cached from the
  window statistics to the end of the model phase; C: those rows and the four
  tables that the phases write and read back, cached until the end of the
  checks. Each cache was filled by an explicit `count()` at
  `MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER` and released after its last reader.
- **Runs.** Six protocols of four fresh-process runs in the order A–B–C–C–B–A,
  in one batch. All 24 runs passed every check, no sample reached the 4.8 GiB
  stop threshold, and the batch met every acceptance criterion, including the
  cache checks: Spark's storage information showed every cache filled in full,
  in memory, and released in its phase, and the plans showed cached reads
  after the fills in every phase meant to have them. The machine checks were
  recorded at every start, and no drift was detected (A +1.2%).
- **Time.** Median times without the plan recording were 26.5 s (A), 27.0 s
  (B) and 28.7 s (C). Overall, B and C were 2.1% and 8.4% slower than A; both
  were slower in each half. Both differences were below the threshold of 10%
  of A's median, so there was no clear difference. Caching the members
  lengthened the window statistics by 0.93 s and shortened the model phase by
  0.33 s; their fill took 2.48 s, building the members included. C's further
  caches lengthened the model phase by 1.29 s against B, with no observed net
  saving in the summaries or checks.
- **Memory and results.** Median peaks were 2.68–2.70 GiB, with no clear
  difference; C held up to about 0.2 GiB in cached tables, all in memory, and
  its JVM peak was 0.03 GiB above A's. Every output matched A's within the
  tolerance: A's runs exactly, while in B and C seven floating-point summary
  columns differed in the last bits (relative at most 6.3e-16). `path_days`
  held the same rows in every run, in another order in 9 of its 40 files in B
  and C; a different order of floating-point addition is a plausible
  explanation, but the mechanism was not established.
- **Predictions.** All three median times and peaks were inside their
  predicted ranges, and the predicted comparisons held. The members' fill took
  longer than predicted (2.48 s against 0.3–1.2 s), exact equality of the
  outputs did not hold in B and C, and C's cached reads gave no observed net
  saving. CPU time and GC were not measured.

## 9. Status summary

| Area | Implemented (prototype, Stages 1–3: SQL analyses, Docker image, stride, shuffle-partition and caching experiments, pandas baseline) | Planned |
|---|---|---|
| Data | download with manifest; five-ticker full-history snapshot; checksum-enforced ingest; calendar, split-day, dividend, zero-volume and flat-bar checks; list of unverified extreme days | second-source comparison; terms-of-use review |
| Model | daily-reset model, breach rule, drawdown, rebalance; hand-calculated tests; daily turnover and realized variance per window (computed in Spark) | — |
| Windows | 252-day rolling windows on a shared NYSE start grid (run at stride 21); calendar-year supplement; full-period windows for the prototype; unverified-day flags over all price dates (conservative rule); self-checked, checksummed definitions with code provenance; strides 14, 7 and 3 built and run for the stride experiment | stride 1 (excluded for now, [experiments.md](experiments.md) 1.3) |
| Spark | window members joined to broadcast returns; one grouped pandas call per window for both leverages; count-guarded Spark summaries; 1x/2x pairing on the window key with pre-breach values kept apart; scheduled vs actual end dates; ten full-scale checks; `verify` sample check; three Spark SQL analyses of the paired results (project author, §8) | — |
| Performance | fresh-process timed runs with process-tree memory sampling and a stop rule; the stride experiment (strides 21, 14 and 7, stride 3 exploratory; Spark defaults; drift detected) and its measurements CSV ([experiments.md](experiments.md)); the shuffle-partition experiment (settings A, B and C at stride 7; one batch meeting every acceptance criterion; no drift) with the partition flags, plan recording with actual partition counts, the batch collector and the session helpers ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)); the pandas baseline (the Spark pipeline against a single-process pandas implementation at stride 7, end to end; one batch meeting every acceptance criterion; no drift) with the pandas pipeline, `measure --pipeline`, the batch collector and the session helpers ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)); the caching experiment (no cache, the window-member rows, and those plus the four read-back tables at stride 7; one batch meeting every acceptance criterion; no drift) with the `--cache` option, cache records and checks from Spark's storage information and the plans, the batch collector and the session helpers ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)) | — |
| Environment | uv lockfile; pandas below 3 for PySpark; pandas-market-calendars 5.5.0, yfinance 1.7.0 and psutil 7.2.2 pinned exactly; Docker image for the pipeline (Python 3.12, Java 17, locked dependencies, base images pinned by digest; data mounted, not copied; commit recorded at build time) | a NumPy pin (pandas 2.3 emits deprecation warnings under NumPy 2.5) |
| Systems extension | — | MySQL job table, Kafka job queue, worker and reconciler, Redis result cache, Docker Compose, recovery and caching experiments (§11) |
| Documentation | README, [data-sources.md](data-sources.md), this specification, [experiments.md](experiments.md), [partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md), [pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md), [caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md), [AI-usage logs](ai-usage/README.md) | design decisions, results, demo script |

## 10. Known issues and open items after the Stage 2 cleanup

- The three prototype problems listed for Stage 2 (the ticker-only join, end
  dates taken from simulated rows, collecting every summary for the reference
  check) are fixed as described in sections 6 and 7.
- The Stage 2 review findings are fixed: the unverified flag now includes the
  entry date (a conservative rule change), partial pre-breach 2x values are
  stored only in `*_pre_breach` columns, check 10 covers every count-guarded
  value in both directions, definitions are self-checked, records carry code
  provenance and the measured JVM heap, pairing refuses leverages other than 1x
  and 2x, and config paths resolve against the repository root. The earlier
  definitions and runs are kept unchanged next to a `SUPERSEDED.txt` note
  pointing to the `-r2` folders.
- Strides 14, 7 and 3 were run in the stride experiment, stride 3 only as an
  exploratory protocol that the experiment's memory rule did not admit; stride
  1 has not been run.
- Performance has been measured on one machine only, with Spark's default
  settings except in the shuffle-partition experiment. In the stride
  experiment the repeated stride-21 protocol's median wall time was 18.3% below
  the first's (drift beyond the 10% tolerance), the apps open during its last
  two protocols are uncertain, and the shuffle partition counts Spark actually
  used, spilling and CPU use were not recorded
  ([experiments.md](experiments.md) 5.3, 5.5, 6.5). The shuffle-partition
  experiment ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md)) recorded the
  partition counts, but its machine checks only before the first protocol,
  and its last protocol followed a two-hour break (14.3); CPU time, spilling
  and GC were not measured. Its code and tests are by Claude Code; its
  predictions were drafted with Claude Code and approved by the project
  author, who ran its formal session and wrote its answers. The pandas
  baseline ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md)) compared the Spark
  pipeline end to end with a single-process pandas implementation at stride 7,
  in one batch that met every acceptance criterion; sharing the model function
  does not isolate Spark's overhead, and only one workload was measured. The
  caching experiment ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md)) compared
  three caching strategies at stride 7 in one batch that met every acceptance
  criterion; under its rule, caching made no clear difference to runtime or
  peak memory for this workload, and CPU time and GC were not measured. The
  three Spark SQL analyses are done (§8).
- 239 of the 1,790 stride-21 windows (13%), and 30% of NVDA's and 33% of TSLA's,
  use the price of an unverified extreme day. Results are also shown without
  them as a **sensitivity analysis**: the flagged windows are a non-random
  subset (periods with extreme market days), so the comparison shows how much
  results depend on those periods, not whether those days are data errors.
- Open transcript-hook items (separator rule, save timing, folders for
  interruption notices) and the NumPy deprecation warnings are unchanged.

## 11. Systems extension — planned (optional)
